questions.question: What is `this` inside a plain function call? Explain the difference between strict mode and sloppy mode, and why the answer depends on the call site.
questions.answer: In a plain call `fn()` there is no receiver, so strict mode leaves `this` as `undefined` and sloppy mode substitutes the global object (`globalThis`, or `window` in a browser). The function body does not decide this; the call site and the mode do. That is why the same function can log `undefined` when called as `fn()` and an object when called as `obj.fn()`.
key_points: Strict plain call: `this === undefined`.
Sloppy plain call: `this` is the global object.
The call site decides `this`, not where the function was written.
ES modules and class bodies are always strict.

questions.question: Why does an arrow function used as an object method fail to see the object, while a normal method works? What does `this` refer to in each case?
questions.answer: An arrow function has no own `this`; it captures the lexical `this` of the scope where it was written. At module or top level that is `undefined`, so `obj.arrow()` cannot read `obj.name`. A method shorthand creates a normal function, and calling it as `obj.method()` sets `this` to `obj` via implicit binding.
key_points: Arrows have no own `this` and cannot be rebound with call/apply/bind.
Method shorthand gets the receiver from `obj.method()`.
Use arrows for callbacks that should inherit the outer `this`.
Use methods or arrow class fields when the function needs its own receiver.

questions.question: Compare `call`, `apply` and `bind`. What does each return, and can a bound `this` be changed afterwards?
questions.answer: `call(thisArg, ...args)` invokes immediately with arguments listed individually and returns the function result. `apply(thisArg, argsArray)` invokes immediately with an array of arguments. `bind(thisArg, ...leadingArgs)` does not invoke; it returns a new function with `this` permanently locked and optional leading arguments pre-filled. A later `call`, `apply`, or `bind` cannot override the bound `this`, though `new` on a bound function creates a fresh object and ignores the bound `this` while keeping the bound arguments.
key_points: call = invoke now, args list; apply = invoke now, args array.
bind = new function, does not invoke.
Bound `this` is permanent; rebinding attempts are ignored.
`new` on a bound function ignores the bound `this` but keeps bound args.

questions.question: Write a function `once(fn)` that returns a wrapper which calls `fn` at most once, preserves the caller's `this` and arguments, and returns the first result on every later call.
key_points: Return a normal `function`, not an arrow, so the caller's `this` survives.
Capture the first arguments with rest parameters and forward with `apply(this, args)`.
Cache the result and return it on later calls.
Later calls must not invoke `fn` again, even with a different receiver.

questions.question: Refactor this class so `click` can be passed directly to `setTimeout` without losing `this`.
key_points: Class methods are strict, so a detached method gets `this === undefined` and throws.
An arrow class field is created per instance with `this` bound to that instance.
Alternatively bind in the constructor: `this.click = this.click.bind(this)`.
Arrow class fields cost one function per instance, which is fine for handlers.

questions.answer: In strict mode (modules and classes) it throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')`. `greet()` is a plain call, so `this` is `undefined`. In sloppy mode it prints `undefined` because `this` becomes the global object, which has no `name`. Storing `user.greet` in a variable drops the implicit binding; fix it with `greet.call(user)` or `user.greet.bind(user)`.
key_points: Assigning a method to a variable removes the receiver.
Strict plain call → `this === undefined` → TypeError on property access.
Sloppy plain call → global object → `undefined` result, not a crash.
Fix with `bind` or by calling `user.greet()` directly.

questions.answer: It logs `Asha`. `new` creates a fresh object and uses it as `this`, so `this.name = 'Kakade'` writes to that object. But when a constructor returns an object, that object replaces the newly created one, so the returned literal wins and the `Kakade` instance is discarded. Returning a primitive would be ignored and the new object would be kept.
key_points: `new` returns the created object by default.
An explicitly returned object overrides the created object.
An explicitly returned primitive is ignored.
This is a common source of surprising constructor behaviour.

questions.answer: It prints `[ 'Kakade:none', 'Asha:none' ]`. `map` invokes its callback as a plain function, so the callback's `this` is `undefined` in strict mode and the optional chain falls back to `'none'`. The outer `list` method has `this === team`, but that binding is not inherited by a normal nested function. Use an arrow callback, or pass `team` as `map`'s second `thisArg`.
key_points: Normal callbacks do not inherit the enclosing method's `this`.
Arrows inherit lexical `this`, so `map((m) => ...)` works.
`map` accepts a `thisArg` second argument for normal callbacks.
Optional chaining hides the bug by returning a fallback instead of throwing.
